flashcards.back: A form of recursion where the recursive call is the last operation in the function.

flashcards.front: Why can tail recursion be optimized?
flashcards.back: No remaining work after the call, so the stack frame can be reused (TCO) when supported.
Use a loop with an accumulator multiplying 1..n.
Input must be sorted (or monotone predicate over index range).

flashcards.front: Give an example algorithm with Θ(n²) runtime.
flashcards.back: Bubble sort / selection sort / insertion sort (worst case).

flashcards.front: Space cost of recursive binary search.
flashcards.back: Θ(log n) call stack; iterative version uses Θ(1) space.
Tail-recursive factorial vs non-tail-recursive naive Fibonacci.

flashcards.front: Insertion Sort runtime in worst vs best case?
Is Insertion Sort stable and in-place?
What is the runtime of MergeSort?
flashcards.back: Θ(n log n) in best, average, and worst cases.

flashcards.front: What extra resource does MergeSort need?

flashcards.back: Average: Θ(n log n), Worst: Θ(n²).

flashcards.front: When does QuickSort hit worst case?
flashcards.back: When partitions are extremely unbalanced (e.g., already sorted input with bad pivot choice).

flashcards.front: Which algorithm is generally faster in practice, MergeSort or QuickSort?
flashcards.back: QuickSort, due to in-place partitioning and better cache behavior.
Decrease-and-conquer reduces to one smaller problem; divide-and-conquer splits into multiple subproblems.

quiz.question: Tail recursion can be optimized by compilers because:
options: The recursive call is the last action and needs no additional stack frame
quiz.explanation: Tail calls can reuse the current frame when supported.

quiz.question: Binary search requires:
quiz.explanation: Typical array binary search assumes random access and sorted order.

quiz.question: Worst-case comparisons for binary search on n elements:
quiz.explanation: Halving the search space yields logarithmic depth.

quiz.question: Which has Θ(n²) time in the worst case?
quiz.explanation: Insertion sort degrades to quadratic when reversed.

quiz.question: The recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+1 solves to:
quiz.explanation: Each level contributes constant work for log n levels.

quiz.question: Space complexity of iterative binary search:
A function is tail-recursive if:
options: It returns the result of the recursive call directly
quiz.explanation: No work after the recursive call.

quiz.question: Comparing growth: which dominates for large n?
quiz.explanation: Quadratic grows much faster than logarithmic.

quiz.question: Which statement is true?
options: Binary search works on any unsorted array.
Binary search’s runtime is Θ(log n) because it halves the search space.
Tail recursion always reduces asymptotic time.
quiz.explanation: Sorting is a precondition; tail recursion affects space/constant factors.

quiz.question: Non-tail-recursive Fibonacci has time:
quiz.explanation: Two recursive branches per level → Θ(φ^n).

quiz.question: Insertion Sort has which time complexity in the worst case?
quiz.explanation: Two nested loops make Insertion Sort quadratic in the worst case.

quiz.question: MergeSort requires extra space because:
options: It merges subarrays using auxiliary arrays
quiz.explanation: MergeSort copies into temporary arrays during merging.

quiz.question: QuickSort’s worst case occurs when:
options: The pivot splits the array evenly
The pivot produces highly unbalanced partitions
quiz.explanation: Unbalanced partitions (like sorted input with poor pivot) lead to Θ(n²).

quiz.question: Which algorithm is stable?
quiz.explanation: MergeSort preserves order of equal keys; QuickSort and HeapSort typically do not.

quiz.question: Decrease-and-conquer differs from divide-and-conquer in that:
options: It reduces to one smaller subproblem
quiz.explanation: Decrease-and-conquer reduces the problem to one smaller subproblem.
